items.title: Post-Kakatiya Andhra: Musunuris, Velamas & Reddis
items.body:
### Andhra after the fall of the Kakatiyas (1323)

**In one line:** When the Kakatiya empire fell in 1323, three Telugu warrior lineages — the Musunuris, the Recherla Velamas and the Reddis — rose to fill the power vacuum.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC often tests who led the Telugu resistance to Delhi, the Vilasa grant, and the recovery of Warangal in 1336. Define once: a *Nayaka* = a military chieftain/commander; a *copper-plate grant* = a royal order engraved on copper sheets, used by historians as evidence.

**The story**

- In **1323** the Delhi Sultanate captured the Kakatiya king **Prataparudra II** and renamed Warangal 'Sultanpur'. But Tughluq control of the far-off Telugu country was weak, and local chiefs soon seized power.
- The **Musunuri Nayakas** led the earliest organised revolt. **Prolaya Nayaka** (around 1330) claimed Kakatiya heritage and issued the **Vilasa copper-plate grant** near Pithapuram, lamenting the land's devastation.
- His cousin **Kapaya Nayaka (r. 1333–1368)** led a wider rising and **recovered Warangal from the Tughluqs in 1336**, reportedly backed by **75 Nayakas** — among them Prolaya Vema Reddi, future founder of the Reddi kingdom.
- Pressed later by the Bahmanis, the Musunuris were **overthrown by the Recherla Velamas in 1368**. Power then settled on two rivals: the **Reddis** in the coastal belt and the **Velamas** in the Telangana uplands.

**Why it matters:** This is the bridge between the Kakatiya and Vijayanagara ages — the 'who ruled Andhra in between?' question, with a strong Telugu-identity theme Mains likes.

**Picture it**

| Lineage | Core region | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Musunuri Nayakas | Coastal Andhra → Warangal | Led the anti-Sultanate revolt |
| Recherla Velamas | Telangana (Rachakonda, Devarakonda) | Rivals of the Reddis |
| Reddis | Coastal & central Andhra (Kondavidu) | Longest-lasting of the three |

**Terms explained**
- **Vilasa grant** = Prolaya Nayaka's copper-plate record describing the ruin after the invasions.
- **Recherla Velamas** = the Telangana warrior line (seats at Rachakonda and Devarakonda) who often allied with the Bahmanis.

**Don't confuse:** The **Reddis rose in coastal/central Andhra** (Addanki, Kondavidu), NOT in Telangana — the Telangana uplands were held by the **Velamas**.

**Remember it:** "1336 = Kapaya + 75 Nayakas win back Warangal."

**TL;DR**
- Kakatiya empire ended 1323 (capture of Prataparudra II); Warangal renamed Sultanpur.
- Three Telugu lineages filled the vacuum: Musunuri Nayakas, Recherla Velamas, Reddis.
- Prolaya Nayaka issued the Vilasa grant (c.1330); Kapaya Nayaka recovered Warangal in 1336 with 75 Nayakas.
- Musunuri power fell to the Recherla Velamas in 1368.
keyPoints: Kakatiya empire ended 1323 (capture of Prataparudra II); Warangal renamed Sultanpur.
Three Telugu lineages filled the vacuum: Musunuri Nayakas, Recherla Velamas, Reddis.

Kapaya Nayaka recovered Warangal from the Tughluqs in 1336, aided by 75 Nayakas.
Musunuri power fell to the Recherla Velamas in 1368.

items.title: The Reddi Kingdom of Kondavidu — Foundation & Rulers
items.body:
### The founding and rulers of the Reddi kingdom

**In one line:** The Reddi kingdom of Kondavidu (c.1325–1448), founded by Prolaya Vema Reddi, was the longest-lasting Telugu successor state in coastal and central Andhra.

**Why it is asked:** The founder, the two capitals, and the scholar-kings are standard AP facts, and the two 'Vema' kings are a classic confusion trap. Define once: *sainya-nayaka* = a military commander; an *agrahara* = a village or land grant given to Brahmins.

**The story**

- The word **'Reddi'** (earlier *Rattakudi/Rattodi*, linked to **Rashtrakuta**) meant a **village headman** who managed cultivation and collected taxes. The founder's family had served as **sainya-nayakas** (commanders) under the Kakatiyas.
- **Prolaya Vema Reddi** of the **Panta Reddi clan** set up independent rule around **1325**, first ruling from **Addanki**.
- **Anavota (Anapota) Reddi** consolidated the state and moved the capital to the strong hill-fort of **Kondavidu** (in today's Guntur district) — which is why the dynasty is usually called the Kondavidu Reddis.
- **Anavema Reddi** boosted trade by **abolishing customs duties**. The scholar-king **Kumaragiri Reddi (r. c.1386–1402)** wrote the dance treatise **Vasantarajiyam**, and **Peda Komati Vema Reddi** was the patron of the great poet **Srinatha**.

**Why it matters:** Kondavidu was the political and literary heart of 14th–15th century Andhra — a core AP-history topic for both Prelims and Mains.

**Picture it**

| Ruler | Known for |
|---|---|
| Prolaya Vema Reddi (c.1325–1353) | Founder; temple-builder; patron of Errana |
| Anavota Reddi | Shifted capital to Kondavidu |
| Anavema Reddi | Abolished customs duties |
| Kumaragiri Reddi (c.1386–1402) | Scholar-king; wrote Vasantarajiyam |
| Peda Komati Vema Reddi | Patron of Srinatha |

**Terms explained**
- **Panta Reddi clan** = the specific Reddi sub-group to which the founders belonged.
- **Apratima-Bhudana-Parasurama** = Prolaya Vema Reddi's title, 'the Parasurama of matchless land-gifts'.

**Don't confuse:** **Prolaya Vema Reddi** (the founder, patron of **Errana**) is a different king from **Peda Komati Vema Reddi** (a later Kondavidu ruler, patron of **Srinatha**).

**Remember it:** Two 'Vema' patrons — Prolaya Vema → Errana; Peda Komati Vema → Srinatha.

**TL;DR**
- 'Reddi' derives from Rattakudi/Rashtrakuta — village headmen; founder's line were sainya-nayakas under the Kakatiyas.
- Prolaya Vema Reddi (Panta clan) founded the kingdom c.1325 with Addanki as first capital.
- Anavota Reddi shifted the capital to the Kondavidu hill-fort (Guntur district).
- Kumaragiri Reddi (c.1386–1402) wrote Vasantarajiyam; Prolaya Vema patronised Errana, Peda Komati Vema patronised Srinatha.
keyPoints: 'Reddi' derives from Rattakudi/Rashtrakuta — village headmen; founder's line were sainya-nayakas under the Kakatiyas.

items.title: Rajahmundry Branch, Forts & Extent
items.body:
### The Rajahmundry branch, the forts and the kingdom's extent

**In one line:** A second Reddi line ruled from Rajahmundry on the Godavari, and the kingdom as a whole was defended by famous hill-forts and once stretched from Odisha to Kanchi.

**Why it is asked:** The Rajahmundry branch, the forts (Kondavidu, Kondapalli) and the north–south extent are frequent map/match questions. Define once: a *hill-fort* = a fortress built on a hill for defence; a *doab* here just means the fertile land between the Krishna and Godavari.

**The story**

- Around **1395** a **subsidiary Reddi branch was set up at Rajahmundry (Rajamahendravaram)** on the Godavari, which later became independent. Its rulers included **Kataya Vema Reddi**, the powerful regent **Allada Reddi**, and **Virabhadra Reddi**, who patronised **Srinatha** in the poet's later years.
- The Reddis were celebrated **fort-builders**. The two great surviving hill-forts are **Kondavidu** (about 30 km west of Guntur) and **Kondapalli** (about 20 km north-west of Vijayawada). The **Palnadu** forts of **Bellamkonda, Vinukonda and Nagarjunakonda** also lay within the kingdom.
- At its greatest extent the kingdom reached from **Cuttack/Simhachalam in the north to Kanchi in the south, with Srisailam to the west**; its heartland lay between the **Krishna and Godavari** rivers, with the sea-port of **Motupalli** on the coast.

**Why it matters:** This fixes the geography of Reddi power — the forts and ports that let a regional kingdom survive a century of pressure.

**Picture it**

| Fort | Location |
|---|---|
| Kondavidu | West of Guntur (capital) |
| Kondapalli | Near Vijayawada |
| Bellamkonda / Vinukonda / Nagarjunakonda | Palnadu region |

**Terms explained**
- **Rajamahendravaram** = the older name of Rajahmundry, seat of the junior Reddi branch.
- **Simhachalam** = a hill shrine near Visakhapatnam marking the kingdom's northern reach.

**Don't confuse:** **Addanki** was the *first* capital of the main line; **Kondavidu** was the fortified capital; **Rajahmundry** was the *branch* capital (from 1395) — three different seats.

**Remember it:** "Two forts, one port — Kondavidu and Kondapalli guard the land, Motupalli opens the sea."

**TL;DR**
- A Reddi branch was set up at Rajahmundry c.1395 and later became independent.
- Rajahmundry rulers: Kataya Vema, Allada Reddi and Virabhadra Reddi (patron of Srinatha).
- Chief Reddi forts: Kondavidu (west of Guntur) and Kondapalli (near Vijayawada); Palnadu forts Bellamkonda, Vinukonda, Nagarjunakonda.
- Maximum extent: Cuttack (N) to Kanchi (S), Srisailam (W); core between Krishna and Godavari.
keyPoints: A Reddi branch was set up at Rajahmundry c.1395 and later became independent.
Rajahmundry rulers: Kataya Vema, Allada Reddi and Virabhadra Reddi (patron of Srinatha).
Chief Reddi forts: Kondavidu (west of Guntur) and Kondapalli (near Vijayawada).
Palnadu forts Bellamkonda, Vinukonda and Nagarjunakonda were also Reddi.

items.title: Reddi Administration, Trade & Religion
items.body:
### How the Reddis governed, traded and worshipped

**In one line:** The Reddis ran a Dharmasutra-based state with a light land tax and lively sea trade, and were energetic patrons of Hindu temples.

**Why it is asked:** The one-sixth tax, the Motupalli port, and the Srisailam/Ahobilam patronage are reliable AP facts, often linked to the 'Hindu revival' theme. Define once: *Dharmasutras* = ancient Hindu texts of law and duty used as a guide to governance; *kula-devi* = a family's tutelary (guardian) goddess.

**The story**

- **Administration and economy:** government followed the **Dharmasutras**, and the state took **one-sixth of the agricultural surplus** as land tax — a traditional, moderate rate. Under **Anavota/Anavema Reddi, customs and trade duties were lifted**, so commerce grew and **sea trade flowed through the port of Motupalli**, which attracted a large merchant community.
- **Religion:** the Reddis were **staunch patrons of Hinduism**, restoring Brahmin **agraharas**, promoting Vedic learning, and endowing the temples of **Srisailam, Tirumala, Ahobilam and Vontimitta**.
- **Prolaya Vema Reddi** built a **flight of steps** from the Krishna River up to the **Srisailam Mallikarjuna** temple, repaired that shrine, built the **Ahobilam Narasimha** temple, and is credited with **108 Siva temples**.
- The dynasty's **kula-devi was Mullamguramma**, a village goddess later identified with **Uma (Parvati)**.

**Why it matters:** This is the evidence base for calling the Reddis champions of a Hindu cultural revival after the invasions — a favourite Mains argument.

**Terms explained**
- **Agrahara** = a tax-free land/village grant to Brahmins to support learning and ritual.
- **Mullamguramma** = the Reddis' family goddess, later merged with Uma/Parvati.

**Don't confuse:** The Reddi land tax was **one-sixth** of produce (the traditional *shadbhaga*), not one-third; and they **encouraged** maritime trade through Motupalli rather than restricting it.

**Remember it:** "One-sixth tax, free ports at Motupalli, and steps to Srisailam."

**TL;DR**
- Administration followed the Dharmasutras; land tax was one-sixth of the surplus.
- Anavota/Anavema Reddi abolished customs/trade duties, boosting commerce.
- Sea trade flowed through the port of Motupalli.
- Reddis endowed Srisailam, Tirumala, Ahobilam and Vontimitta temples; kula-devi was Mullamguramma (later Uma/Parvati).
keyPoints: Administration followed the Dharmasutras; land tax was one-sixth of the surplus.
Anavota/Anavema Reddi abolished customs/trade duties, boosting commerce.
Sea trade flowed through the port of Motupalli.
Reddis endowed Srisailam, Tirumala, Ahobilam and Vontimitta temples and Brahmin agraharas.
Kula-devi of the Reddis was Mullamguramma, later identified with Uma/Parvati.

items.title: Telugu Literature under the Reddis — Errana & Srinatha
items.body:
### The golden age of Telugu letters under the Reddis

**In one line:** Reddi patronage produced a golden age of Telugu literature, crowned by Errana (third of the Kavitraya) and Srinatha (the 'Emperor of Poets').

**Why it is asked:** The Kavitraya trio, Errana's Aranya Parva, and Srinatha's titles and works are among the most tested AP-literature facts. Define once: *Kavitraya* = the 'trinity of poets' who created the Telugu Mahabharata; *prabandha* = a highly ornate Telugu narrative poem.

**The story**

- **Errana (Errapragada)** was the **court poet of Prolaya Vema Reddi** and the **third member of the Kavitraya** (after Nannaya and Tikkana). He **completed the Aranya Parva** of the Telugu Mahabharata that Nannaya had left unfinished, skilfully blending Nannaya's and Tikkana's styles. He also wrote the **Nrisimha Puranamu** and **Harivamsamu**, and held the titles **'Prabandha Parameswara'** and **'Sambhudasa'**.
- **Srinatha** was the colossus of the age. He served as **Vidyadhikari (education officer) at Kondavidu under Peda Komati Vema Reddi**, and won the title **'Kavi Sarvabhauma'** (Emperor of Poets) with a **Kanakabhishekam** (ceremonial shower of gold) at the **Vijayanagara court of Praudha Devaraya**, after defeating the scholar **Dindima Bhattu**. His works include **Sringara Naishadhamu** (a Telugu rendering of Sri Harsha's Naishadhiya Charitam), **Bhimakhandamu, Kasikhandamu, Haravilasamu** and the folk-epic **Palnati Vira Charitra**. He later served the Rajahmundry Reddi **Virabhadra**.
- The poet **Bammera Potana**, author of the Telugu **Bhagavatamu**, also belonged to this age.

**Why it matters:** This is the heart of the AP syllabus clause on the Kavitraya and medieval Telugu literature — high-value for both Prelims and Mains.

**Terms explained**
- **Vidyadhikari** = the officer in charge of education/learning at the Reddi court.
- **Kanakabhishekam** = a royal honour of pouring gold over a poet to reward supreme skill.

**Don't confuse:** **Errana** completed the **Aranya Parva** (the part Nannaya left unfinished); **Srinatha** is linked to **Peda Komati Vema** and Vijayanagara's **Praudha Devaraya**, not to the founder Prolaya Vema.

**Remember it:** Kavitraya = Nannaya, Tikkana, Errana (N-T-E).

**TL;DR**
- Errana, court poet of Prolaya Vema Reddi, completed the Aranya Parva and is the third of the Kavitraya.
- Errana's titles: Prabandha Parameswara and Sambhudasa; works Nrisimha Puranamu and Harivamsamu.
- Srinatha was Vidyadhikari at Kondavidu under Peda Komati Vema Reddi.
- Srinatha won 'Kavi Sarvabhauma' and Kanakabhishekam at Praudha Devaraya's court; works include Sringara Naishadhamu and Palnati Vira Charitra.
keyPoints: Errana, court poet of Prolaya Vema Reddi, completed the Aranya Parva and is the third of the Kavitraya.
Errana's titles: Prabandha Parameswara and Sambhudasa; works Nrisimha Puranamu and Harivamsamu.
Srinatha was Vidyadhikari at Kondavidu under Peda Komati Vema Reddi.

items.title: Decline of the Reddis & the Gajapatis of Kalinga
items.body:
### The fall of the Reddis and the Gajapati contest

**In one line:** Squeezed between Vijayanagara, the Velama–Bahmani combine and the Gajapatis of Odisha, the Reddi kingdoms fell by the mid-15th century, after which the Gajapatis and Vijayanagara fought over coastal Andhra.

**Why it is asked:** The two end-dates (Kondavidu 1424, Rajahmundry c.1448), the Gajapati founder, and the 'four royal titles' are common AP facts. Define once: *Suryavamsa* = the 'solar dynasty' line of the Gajapatis; the *Jagannath cult* = the worship of Lord Jagannath (a form of Vishnu) centred at Puri.

**The story**

- The Reddis were caught between three powers: **Vijayanagara** to the south-west, the **Recherla Velamas with their Bahmani allies**, and the **Gajapatis** to the north.
- **Kondavidu was annexed by the Vijayanagara Empire in 1424**; the **Rajahmundry branch was conquered by the Gajapatis of Odisha around 1448**, closing the kingdom's roughly **1325–1448** span.
- The **Gajapati kingdom** was founded by **Kapilendra Deva in 1434** (the Suryavamsa line) after the end of the **Eastern Gangas**, with its capital at **Kataka (Cuttack)**. **'Gajapati' (lord of elephants)** was one of the **four royal titles** of medieval India — the others being **Narapati** (Vijayanagara), **Aswapati** (Bahmani sultans) and **Chhatrapati**.
- The Gajapatis were ardent **Vaishnavas** who expanded the **Jagannath cult**; **Chaitanya Mahaprabhu** influenced Emperor **Prataparudra Deva**. They briefly held coastal Andhra, but lost it when **Prataparudra Deva was defeated by Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara**.

**Why it matters:** This closes the medieval-Andhra story and connects it to Vijayanagara — exactly the sweep the AP Mains clause asks for.

**Picture it**

| Event | Approx. date |
|---|---|
| Vijayanagara annexes Kondavidu | 1424 |
| Gajapati kingdom founded (Kapilendra Deva) | 1434 |
| Gajapatis take Rajahmundry | c.1448 |

**Terms explained**
- **Kataka** = Cuttack, the Gajapati capital in Odisha.
- **Four royal titles** = Gajapati, Narapati, Aswapati, Chhatrapati — the elephant-, man-, horse- and umbrella-lords.

**Don't confuse:** **Kondavidu** fell to **Vijayanagara (1424)**, while **Rajahmundry** fell to the **Gajapatis (c.1448)** — two different conquerors, two different dates.

**Remember it:** Four royal titles — "Gaja (elephant), Nara (man), Aswa (horse), Chhatra (umbrella)."

**TL;DR**
- Kondavidu annexed by Vijayanagara in 1424; Rajahmundry taken by the Gajapatis c.1448.
- Reddi kingdom's overall span was c.1325–1448.
- Gajapati kingdom founded by Kapilendra Deva (1434), capital Kataka (Cuttack).
- 'Gajapati' was one of four royal titles (Gajapati, Narapati, Aswapati, Chhatrapati); Prataparudra Deva was defeated by Krishnadevaraya.
keyPoints: Kondavidu annexed by Vijayanagara in 1424; Rajahmundry taken by the Gajapatis c.1448.

items.title: For Mains — The Reddi Kingdoms & Medieval Andhra
items.body:
## For Mains — The Reddi Kingdoms & Medieval Andhra (Paper-II, clause M2-7)

This is a flagship AP-history Mains topic (medieval Andhra 1000–1565, Telugu literature, Kakatiya successors). Mains asks you to *argue* the Reddis' significance — as agents of political recovery and Hindu-Telugu cultural revival — not merely to list kings.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Political recovery | Reddis (and Musunuris) restored Telugu self-rule after 1323; defensible fort-state (Kondavidu, Kondapalli); extent Cuttack–Kanchi. |
| Administration & economy | Dharmasutra governance, light one-sixth land tax, abolition of customs duties, Motupalli sea trade. |
| Cultural / Hindu revival | Agraharas, Srisailam steps, 108 Siva temples, patronage of Tirumala/Ahobilam — a conscious revival after the invasions. |
| Telugu literary golden age | Errana (Aranya Parva, third of the Kavitraya), Srinatha ('Kavi Sarvabhauma'), scholar-kings (Kumaragiri's Vasantarajiyam). |
| Place in the longue durée | Bridge between the Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara; squeezed out by Vijayanagara (1424) and the Gajapatis (1448). |

**Data points and authorities to quote:** founding c.1325 (Prolaya Vema Reddi, Panta clan, Addanki→Kondavidu); the Vilasa grant and Kapaya Nayaka's 1336 recovery of Warangal; Errana completing the Aranya Parva; Srinatha's Kanakabhishekam at Praudha Devaraya's court; one-sixth land tax and Motupalli; end-dates 1424 and c.1448; Gajapati Kapilendra Deva (1434) and the four royal titles.

**Use in answers:**
- *Example:* use the Reddi restoration of Srisailam and patronage of Errana to show that political revival and cultural revival went hand in hand in post-Kakatiya Andhra.
- *Quote:* the Vilasa grant's lament over the devastation of the Telugu country, to set the 'revival' theme.
- *Diagram idea:* a timeline 1323 → 1336 (Warangal recovered) → c.1325–1448 (Reddis) → 1424/1448 (absorption), overlaid on a coastal-Andhra map with Kondavidu, Rajahmundry and Motupalli.
- *AP link:* this entire topic IS the AP angle — the Kavitraya and the Reddi courts are foundational to Andhra Pradesh's literary heritage.
keyPoints: Argue the Reddis as agents of both political recovery and Hindu-Telugu cultural revival after 1323, not a king-list.
Economy/administration to cite: Dharmasutra rule, one-sixth tax, abolished customs, Motupalli sea trade.
Literary golden age: Errana (Aranya Parva, Kavitraya) and Srinatha ('Kavi Sarvabhauma', Kanakabhishekam).
Place in the longue durée: a bridge between the Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara, ended by Vijayanagara (1424) and the Gajapatis (1448).
This topic is itself the core AP angle — foundational to Andhra Pradesh's literary and temple heritage.
